pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 1. Bowls sold: 84. Weather: cold and steamy. Ama's mood: fine.*

Before you see the Lantern Lane Night Market, you smell it. First comes the smoke from Uncle Feng's oyster omelets, then sugar burning on Auntie Ping's tea machine, and then, underneath everything, a deep brown smell like a warm coat. That is star anise, soy sauce, ginger and beef, plus forty years of my grandmother refusing to write anything down.

That last smell is our stall.

I was eleven that winter, and I want it on the record that I loved the market. I loved the long lane of stalls under strings of red and yellow lanterns. I loved the way it woke up at five o'clock like a giant yawning, and the way it did not go to sleep until nearly midnight. I only did not love smelling like it at school.

But that comes later. On the night this story starts, I still thought the smell was just the smell of home.
pages.image: A long lively night-market lane at dusk under strings of glowing red and yellow paper lanterns, stalls with steaming pots and smoking grills on both sides, families strolling, warm golden light and rising steam, with a small girl in a dark green padded jacket walking into the picture from the foreground. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
Our stall is number nineteen, halfway down on the left, and it has four small tables, a lot of plastic stools and one enormous pot. Chen Ama's Beef Noodles. Ama has run it every night since before my father learned to drive.

Ama is my father's mother. She is small and sturdy, with short silver curls, a flowery padded vest, socks inside plastic sandals and a towel permanently over one shoulder. When she cooks, she hums an old song that has no words, or if it has any, she has never told me.

She says hello to every single person the same way. "Chia̍h-pá-buē?" she says. It means *Have you eaten yet?* in Hokkien, which is the language Ama grew up speaking. She says it to regulars, she says it to the mailman, and she says it to people who have plainly just finished a whole omelet.

"Ama," I tell her, "you can't ask everyone if they've eaten."

"Why not?" says Ama. "It is the only question that matters."
pages.image: Ama, a small sturdy grandmother with short silver curls, a flowery padded vest, an apron and a towel over one shoulder, stands smiling at a huge steaming pot at a busy street stall with four small tables and plastic stools, while a few customers wait with empty bowls.

pages.text:
My jobs at the stall are simple. I wipe the tables, carry the bowls, count everything, and keep the ledger. The ledger is a fat red notebook with a rubber band around it, and I write down how many bowls we sold, what the weather was like, and, because Ama insists, how she was feeling.

That night was the Winter Solstice, the shortest day of the year. Ama says that on the solstice a person becomes a year older, no matter when their birthday is, so between customers she gave me a bowl of tangyuan, which are little round rice balls in hot ginger syrup, pink and white and chewy.

"Round," said Ama, tapping the bowl with her chopstick. "So the family stays together."

I counted the tangyuan, out of habit. There were nine. I ate seven slowly, because they were hot, and two quickly, because they were delicious, and I did not think about anything at all. I would like to say it was the last time I felt that way for a while.
pages.image: Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, sits on a plastic stool at a stall table eating a bowl of pink and white rice balls in syrup while her grandmother taps the bowl with a chopstick.

pages.text:
It was a good night, one of those nights when the lane seems to hum. Uncle Feng, who is round and loud and makes oyster omelets at stall seventeen, shouted a joke across the aisle that I am not allowed to repeat. Auntie Ping, who sells bubble tea with glittery nails and a headband with two tiny pom-poms, slid a free tea onto our counter "for the accountant" and winked at me. Old Mr. Gao's shrimp-fishing pond splashed at the end of the row, and a tourist with a camera pointed at our pot.

Ama ladled a small taste into a paper cup and held it out. "Taste first," she said. "Talk later."

The tourist tasted. Then she took another cup. Then she sat down at table two and ordered a whole bowl, which is what happens to almost everybody.

By nine o'clock I had written 84 in the ledger, which was the best number of the month. I remember being so proud of it that I nearly forgot to be tired.
pages.image: A lively stretch of the night market: round Uncle Feng in a bandana flipping omelets at a sizzling griddle and laughing, Auntie Ping with sparkly nails and pom-pom headband handing a bubble tea across a counter, and Ama giving a tourist with a camera a small paper cup of soup to taste.

pages.text:
At closing time, when the lanterns were starting to sway in the cold, the chairman of the market association walked down the lane with a piece of paper and a roll of tape. He pinned it to the board outside the little temple at the end of the row, and stepped back, and did not say a word.

I read it over the shoulder of an old man in a woolly hat. It said that a big new mall called Sky Mall would open after the New Year, and that, after the Lantern Festival, the city would review whether Lantern Lane Night Market should be allowed to stay open.

Review is a polite word. I knew that even then.

I turned back to look at our stall. Steam rose from the pot into the cold air and the lanterns, and for the first time in my whole life, I felt the entire lane hold its breath.
pages.image: At the end of a lantern-lit night-market lane, Lin, a small girl in a green padded jacket, reads a notice pinned to a wooden board beside a small red-roofed temple, standing behind an old man in a woolly hat, while far behind her the stalls glow and steam rises into the cold air.
